analysis.one_liner: Gives debit and check card users the same fraud and dispute protections as credit cards.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee, drew no cosponsors, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have capped what a debit or check card user owes when a card is lost or stolen at $50, the same limit credit card users already have, instead of the current rules that can leave them on the hook for up to $500 if they report late. It would also have let consumers dispute charges for goods that never arrived or weren't accepted, and use some claims and defenses against the card issuer itself. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Debit and check card users — more than 80% of American households by the bill's own findings — gain stronger protection when cards are lost or stolen, since the maximum they could owe for unauthorized transfers would drop from $500 to $50 and the fine print letting banks deny reimbursement for late reports would be repealed. Consumers would also gain the right to have the bank reverse charges for goods or services that were never delivered or not accepted, and could raise certain claims or defenses against the card issuer itself in disputes over transactions over $50. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Caps a consumer's liability for unauthorized debit or check card transfers at the regular $50 limit, repealing both the $500 cap for late-reported transfers and the provision letting banks deny reimbursement when a consumer fails to report an unauthorized transfer or account error in time.

Adds charges for goods or services the consumer never accepted or never received, in line with the agreement made at the time of the transaction, to the list of billing errors consumers can formally dispute with their bank.

Gives cardholders the right to assert claims and defenses (other than tort claims) against the issuer of an accepted card for transactions over $50 where they first tried to resolve the problem with the merchant, with the cap removed when the merchant is affiliated with or solicited by the card issuer.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other debit and check card issuers would absorb more fraud losses and dispute-handling costs: they could no longer limit reimbursement exposure at $500 for late-reported fraud, would have to resolve more categories of disputed charges, and could be drawn into merchant disputes. Some of that cost would likely be passed back to consumers through account fees. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The added fraud losses and dispute-processing costs would fall on banks and card issuers, which could pass them along to all account holders through higher fees, so even careful consumers might pay something.

Repealing the penalty for failing to report an unauthorized transfer or error promptly removes one incentive for consumers to review statements quickly, which could increase total fraud losses in the system.

The new claims-and-defenses right is narrow: it does not apply to transactions of $50 or less, generally requires the consumer to have tried to resolve the problem with the merchant first, and in most cases applies only to transactions made in the consumer's home state or within 100 miles of it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is real and direct: a $50 fraud cap matching credit cards, dispute rights for undelivered goods, and leverage against card issuers. The costs — somewhat higher fraud losses and dispute handling for banks, possibly passed back as fees — are modest by comparison with the $2.75 billion in debit and ATM fraud losses the bill cites for 2005 alone. The bill's main weakness is that it arrived with no cosponsors and no committee activity, so its design was never tested or refined in the legislative process. [S3]

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2006, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Hillary Clinton introduced the bill on September 28, 2006, near the end of the 109th Congress, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No cosponsors ever signed on, and the committee took no further action on the bill — no markup, no vote — before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and debit card issuers are better off because the bill died: they avoided a lower fraud-liability cap, broader dispute rights for cardholders, and new claims-and-defenses exposure against card issuers.

for.name: Hillary Rodham Clinton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Richard Shelby
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair in the 109th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other senator cosponsored, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no measurable party split.

industries.industry: Consumer banks and debit card issuers
industries.note: Issuers would owe cardholders up to $50 instead of up to $500 for unauthorized transfers, could no longer deny reimbursement for late reports, and would have to resolve more disputed charges. The bill's own findings cite $2.75 billion in debit and ATM fraud losses in 2005, part of which would shift from consumers to issuers.

industries.industry: Payment card networks (Visa and Mastercard debit)
industries.note: Stronger consumer dispute and chargeback-style rights could increase network dispute-processing volumes, but also make debit cards more trustworthy for users, potentially supporting usage growth.

Merchants would face more disputed charges reversed for undelivered or unaccepted goods, but would also benefit from consumers who trust debit cards more when fraud losses no longer fall on the cardholder.
